19707-one-wonderful-night-a-romance-of-n:
One Wonderful Night calls itself a romance of New York. Its early pages picture wealth in the millions and a police chief honored at a banquet. A half million a year buys the bliss the scene describes. New York romance novels of this era loved that scale. Money, society, and one compressed night drive the form.

The single-night frame is the book's real device. Everything must change between dusk and dawn. That pressure suits romance, where a meeting can remake a life. The city supplies speed, crowds, and bright rooms. Readers of the time bought such stories as escape. The novel is a sample of popular New York romance before the pulp era.
20107-denmark:
Denmark, in this travel account, opens with its capital city, Copenhagen. The city is large and thriving, with all the marks of a trade capital. It has a mood of friendliness and gaiety all its own. English visitors, the book says, feel at home in merry Copenhagen at once.

From the capital, such accounts move to towns, coasts, and Danish customs. Readers of the era wanted clear facts mixed with warm local color. The book gives them streets, people, and scenes in a brisk tour. It serves now as a snapshot of Denmark as foreign guests then saw it.
20546-the-hand-in-the-dark:
The Hand in the Dark, published in 1920, is a mystery novel built around an old house with a violent past. The house was rebuilt by the freebooter who had burnt it down. That man, Philip Heredith, traced his line to a knight in the Domesday Book.

His ancestor's name stands among the knights of Duke William's army, which gathered at Dives before the Norman Conquest. With nine centuries of blood behind its walls, the house is ripe for secrets. The novel mixes that deep past with a modern crime, in the country-house mystery style of its day.
20556-lamarck-the-founder-of-evolution-h:
Alpheus S. Packard wrote this life of Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, the French naturalist who taught evolution before Darwin. Packard, himself a zoologist, gathered Lamarck's story and his writings on organic evolution. Lamarck's own country, he argues, never forgot him.

His countrymen called the author of the Flore Française the French Linnaeus. The writer of the great work on invertebrate animals took at once the highest rank as the leading zoologist of his period. Yet Lamarck died poor and blind. Packard's book presses his claim as the true founder of the evolution idea.
20776-encyclopedia-of-needlework:
Colour and cloth choices open the Encyclopedia of Needlework, a vast guide to hand work. Notes by each plate help readers pick shades and threads with ease. Most patterns were worked in D.M.C. cottons, praised here as the best of their kind.

Stitch by stitch, the book covers embroidery, lace, crochet, knitting, and more. Therese de Dillmont built this guide from years of teaching and design. It became the standard needlework book in homes across Europe and America. Crafters still raid its plates for classic patterns, proof of how clear and full its teaching remains.
21052-the-pirate-shark:
A serious lad in a smudgy mechanic's cap and greasy overalls fronts The Pirate Shark. Keen grey eyes, a firm chin, and straight black hair mark him a worker. An onlooker might judge him a stubborn fighter if need arose, the text adds.

H. Bedford-Jones and W. C. Tuttle fill this tale with ships, sharks, and sea peril. A young mechanic's grit meets a pirate threat on wild waters. Pulp pace rules each chapter, with peril and pluck in fast turns. The book is a brisk fossil of magazine adventure, when a boy with a wrench could stand between a ship and its doom.
22000-kept-in-the-dark:
A kept secret poisons a marriage in Anthony Trollope's Kept in the Dark, his last novel, published in 1882. Cecilia Holt lives happily at Exeter with her widowed mother, in a house with a garden, a brougham, and two boys to tend it. An early engagement to the worthless Sir Francis Geraldine ends, and Mr. Western offers her a second chance. What all her friends said about it fills a chapter, as Trollope's titles like to do.

Cecilia does not tell her new husband about the old engagement, and what is kept in the dark works its harm. Miss Altifiorla, the tale's sharp guest, stirs every pot she touches. Trollope died during the serial run in Good Words. Even unfinished in the public eye, the novel shows his fairness and his lifelong theme: pride and concealment in love.
22646-the-hunters-of-the-ozark:
Edward S. Ellis wrote The Hunters of the Ozark, a frontier adventure for boys published in 1887. Ellis was one of the most prolific dime novelists in America, and his tales of the border country taught generations of boys their idea of the wild West. The Ozark hills of Missouri and Arkansas give this one its ground.

One autumn day, Terence Clark urges his friend Frederick Linden to hunt for a cow missing since the night before. With his mother's consent, Frederick joins, and the search becomes the most eventful the two lads had ever known. Lost stock leads to wild country and wilder company, as Ellis's formula promised. The book is a clean specimen of the nineteenth-century juvenile frontier tale.
22731-tin-types-taken-in-the-streets-of-:
Tin Types Taken in the Streets of New York is a collection of character sketches of metropolitan life, issued by O. M. Dunham. The catalog record gives no year. Tin types were cheap photographs, and the title promises the verbal equivalent: quick, sharp portraits of the New York types a walker meets daily.

The sample describes one unforgettable nose. It is sharp, thin, hanging, and exceedingly ample. It comes inquiringly out of its owner's face, as if the other features had hired it as a picket sentinel. Such comic physiognomy fills the sketches, which range over newsboys, sharpers, clerks, and cranks. Books of street types were a nineteenth-century staple, half humor and half social survey. This one preserves the city's crowd as its wits saw it.
23113-to-my-younger-brethren-chapters-on:
Handley Moule closes To My Younger Brethren with an envoi on holiness. Reviewing his chapters, Moule lands on one closing thought. A ministry works rightly only through the minister's personal holiness, he writes. Not a shape pressed from outside, but a life growing outward into action.

Moule, Bishop of Durham, addressed these chapters on pastoral life and work to younger clergy. Preaching, visiting, study, and prayer get practical counsel from a scholar-bishop who had trained ministers himself. The tone is earnest and fatherly throughout. The book survives as a window into Anglican ministry at its Victorian-Edwardian height, when character was held to be the clergy's first credential.
a-dark-night-s-work:
Elizabeth Gaskell opens in Hamley, a small county town, where Mr. Wilkins the attorney dines with the gentry his family has served for three generations. His son Edward inherits the practice and the standing, and marries a woman above the family's habits. One dark night, a quarrel in the Wilkins household ends in a killing.

The rest of the novella follows the hiding of that night's work and the long weight it lays on Edward and on Dixon, the loyal servant who shares the secret. A daughter grows up under its shadow. Gaskell, writing in the 1896 collection used here, turns a crime story into a study of guilt eating a respectable life from inside.
after-dark:
Wilkie Collins strings his short tales on a single thread in this collection, as his preface explains. The frame is Leah's diary: Leah is the wife of a traveling portrait painter who is losing his sight. While he rests his eyes, friends and sitters tell stories, which Leah writes down to earn money.

The tales between the diary entries run to mystery, crime, and strange adventure, each with its own prologue from the painter. Ghostly warnings, hidden identities, and narrow escapes fill the pages. Collins, a master of suspense, built the frame with real care, so the frame story itself, about art, poverty, and a wife's devotion, holds its own beside the tales.
beverly-of-graustark: George Barr McCutcheon returns to his imaginary kingdom of Graustark, where the American girl Beverly Calhoun finds herself entangled in royal romance and intrigue. Palace balls, daring escapes, and a prince in disguise fill this cheerful Ruritanian adventure. Pure romantic escapism from the master of the genre.

govdocs-archive_org-man-and-technics-osw:
Oswald Spengler, author of The Decline of the West, published Man and Technics in 1931 as a short contribution to a philosophy of life. Its subject is technology, which Spengler treats not as a neutral tool but as the driving tactic of human existence.

He argues that technics began with the predator's way of life. It reached its peak in Faustian Western man, whose machine culture he expects to turn destructive and to spread beyond its makers' control. The book compresses Spengler's dark view of history into a few chapters. It remains his most read short work on the machine age.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIFeltWMark_FB: W. Mark Felt, once a senior FBI official, appeared on the CBS News program Face the Nation on August 29, 1976. The archived record preserves that broadcast appearance under his name. The file gives the program, the network, and the date. It gives no transcript detail in the surviving evidence. govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WeissMark_Weiss: Harold Weisberg wrote on April 28, 1983, to Barger, Aschkenasy, and Weiss about his FBI Freedom of Information lawsuits. life-and-travels-of-mungo-park:
Mungo Park's travels in Africa anchor this combined life and narrative. Contents begin with what ancients and Arabs knew of the continent. Park trained as a surgeon before the African Association engaged him. His preparations and departure from the Gambia River follow.

Park reached Pisania, the British factory on the river. Sickness struck him there before he set out for the interior. Later chapters promise a full narrative of subsequent central African adventure. The book preserves the record of a famed early African explorer. Ledyard, Lucas, and Houghton precede Park among Africa's English explorers. Portuguese and English discoveries frame the introduction's survey.
making-both-ends-meet-the-income-and-out:
Making Both Ends Meet studies how New York working girls lived on their wages. Sue Ainslie Clark and Edith Wyatt wrote it for Macmillan in 1911. A photograph by Lewis Hine faces the title page. The authors dedicated the book to Florence Kelley, the reform leader.

The study grew from the Consumers' League's work on laundry labor. Laundry owners met the League to seek a ten-hour day. Clark and Wyatt record real budgets, rents, food, and carfare. Girl after girl tells how her pay falls short of her needs. The book became a classic of Progressive Era reform. It lets working women speak in their own figures.
medoline-selwyn-s-work:
Mrs. J. J. Colter wrote Medoline Selwyn's Work, held in rights in Boston in 1889. Ira Bradley and Company printed the book. A verse at the front urges readers to seize the golden hour.

Mrs. Blake and Oaklands open the tale, and Esmerelda comes third. A funeral, a new skill, and Mr. Winthrop mark the early turns. City life, humble charities, and a Christmas tree fill the middle. Mrs. Le Grande's tale and a changed heart lead toward the close. A helping hand and a pleasant surprise lift the later heads. The tale ends from the depths, after much loss and change.
more-letters-of-charles-darwin-volume-1-:
Francis Darwin and A. C. Seward edited this first volume of their father's further letters. Its subtitle calls it a record of his work in hitherto unpublished letters. The editors dedicate it to Sir Joseph Hooker, Darwin's lifelong friend. A quotation from Darwin thanks Hooker for constant kindness and encouragement.

The preface explains that the Life and Letters of 1887 left much unused. New letters arrived from correspondents including Galton, Huxley, Lyell, and Owen. The Hooker correspondence forms the chief treasure, written with complete freedom. Even Darwin's most technical letters gain personal charm there, the editors say, and this volume begins that record.
more-letters-of-charles-darwin-volume-2-:
Volume Two continues the letters of Charles Darwin edited by Francis Darwin and A. C. Seward. The biographical footnotes for both volumes are gathered at this volume's end. Its opening chapter treats geographical distribution from 1843 to 1882. The letters here run from 1867 onward.

Letter 378 is from Joseph Hooker at Kew, dated January 20, 1867. Island plants and animals, and how species spread, dominate the science of these pages. Darwin argues distribution is key evidence for evolution by natural selection. Readers watch him test the theory against facts from his botanist friend's global network, year by year, in his modest and careful voice.
my-life-and-work:
Henry Ford tells his own life and work with help from Samuel Crowther. The contents open with a bold question: what is the idea? Early chapters trace his beginnings and what he learned about business. Then comes the secret of manufacturing and serving.

Later chapters treat wages, machines and men, and cheap goods. Ford asks why not always have good business, and why be poor. Money, he argues, must be a servant, not a master. Tractors, railroads, and charity all get his plain views. V1 called it a bestseller that put his creed on record, for better and for worse.
nasa-tm-19710001808-manned-space-flight-:
NASA published this account of its Manned Space Flight Network, the chain that tracked Apollo flights. Tracking, command, and talk with the crews were Apollo's vital links with Earth. The network worked in two broad phases for each mission.

Near Earth, a worldwide chain of stations with mid-size antennas did the work. Once a craft passed ten thousand miles out, much larger antennas took over for their power and precision. The network held a dozen ground stations, one ship, and four jet aircraft. All were linked to the Mission Control Center in Houston. It had to give instant, reliable contact from liftoff to splashdown.
new-york: New York is a work by James Fenimore Cooper, the American novelist. The hosted sample holds only a Project Gutenberg header, so it preserves no readable content from the work itself. podcast-joerogan-7HoFQdKD9Rk:
Paranormal creators Sam and Colby join the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1922. The pair built a huge online following by spending nights in haunted houses and filming what happens. Rogan, a skeptic with a soft spot for ghost stories, gives them the floor.

They trade their best ghost-hunting stories, from famous haunted sites to nights that scared them off a location. Rogan asks how they rule out tricks and what they truly believe they caught. The episode is a storyteller's session: part travel log of America's spookiest places, part debate over whether anything out there answers back.
podcast-joerogan-yUsJIcqwARk:
German author Norman Ohler brings his book Blitzed to episode 2183 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Ohler researched how deeply Nazi Germany ran on drugs, from soldiers' meth to Hitler's own injections. His work changed how many readers picture the Third Reich.

Ohler explains how the stimulant Pervitin fueled the early blitzkrieg campaigns. He describes the drug culture around Hitler and his personal doctor's cocktail of shots. Rogan asks how much the highs and crashes shaped decisions that killed millions. History's dark students get a gripping, well-sourced tour of the Wehrmacht's hidden fuel.
religion-in-earnest-a-memorial-of-mrs-ma:
John Lyth wrote this memorial of his mother, Mary Lyth of York, in 1861, and signed his preface from Stetten in Württemberg. He calls the work an act of Christian duty, not of family affection alone. Her steady example and her prayers, he says, taught him as a child that religion is the one business of life.

Lyth warns that readers seeking startling incident or fine writing will find little here. His mother made no claim to learning and her story held no romance. What he offers is the growth of grace in a plain life, and proof of how much decision, plain purpose, and steady conduct can do.
snow-bound-and-other-poems-part-4-from-v:
Poems by John Greenleaf Whittier fill one part of a larger set, sorted here under nature poems, poems of self and memory, and religious poems. The contents list Snow-Bound first, then My Triumph, In School-Days, My Birthday, and Red Riding-Hood. Later heads name Response, At Eventide, Voyage of the Jettie, and My Trust, with an autograph poem and A Legacy in the next group.

Whittier gives Snow-Bound, a winter idyl, to the memory of the home it describes. His note names the folk of the Whittier homestead: father, mother, brother, two sisters, an uncle and aunt, and the district school-master who boarded with them. The half-feared, half-welcome guest, he explains, was Harriet Livermore, a young woman of fine gifts, strong temper, and fervent faith.
songs-of-labor-and-reform-part-5-from-vo: John Greenleaf Whittier's anti-slavery poems stand under the head Songs of Labor and Reform in one part of his works. the-balkans-a-history-of-bulgaria-serbia:
Nevill Forbes, Arnold J. Toynbee, D. Mitrany, and D. G. Hogarth shared the writing of a history covering Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece, Rumania, and Turkey. Contents assign Greece to Toynbee, Rumania to Mitrany, and Turkey to Hogarth. An ethnological map of the Balkan Peninsula is listed.

the-bible-king-james-version-book-41-mar:

Samuel Hopkins Adams opens his novel on a mountainside above the Caribbean Sea. A young American sits in a niche of rock hating the blue water in front of him. He comes daily to the shade and the cool trickle from a crevice, wishing the ocean dry so he can walk home to the United States.
